title: The historic wave of labour unrest that swept India
image_caption: Photos by Zaen Alkazi / Design by Sukruti Anah Staneley
content_html:
{ONE}

MORNINGS ARE TYPICALLY RUSHED at Hosiery Complex NOIDA, a prominent industrial hub in Uttar Pradesh. In the urban village of Yakubpur, thousands of migrant workers wake up in small and windowless rooms, rented from local Gurjar farmers, and get ready for work. They share these rooms with night-shift workers, who return to sleep as their day begins.

These workers—mostly men and women from Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha—stream through the narrow winding lanes of Yakubpur toward their factories. They walk past old homes and temples, past shops that offer medicines, fruits, vegetables, phone recharges, loans and remittance services. The lanes open onto an uneven patch of ground strewn with rubbish, cows and the remnants of agricultural fields. Through the gates of low brick walls, one can see charpais and hookahs. Tractors operated by local farmers blare music as they ferry chaff or metallic parts. Women and children sort through piles of rubbish in a settlement of bamboo and tarpaulin homes. Contractors sit on the ground with copybooks, writing down the names and phone numbers of those looking for work.

title: A stalwart of UP politics reflects on his journey and future prospects
content_html:
Few politicians in Uttar Pradesh have traversed the state’s shifting caste and party equations as extensively as Swami Prasad Maurya. Over the past four decades, he has built a reputation as a formidable voice for the Other Backward Classes and as a sharp critic of Hindutva politics.

Swami Prasad began his political journey with the Lok Dal before joining the Janata Dal, in 1991. Five years later, he defected to the Bahujan Samaj Party, where he would go on to become one of party supremo Mayawati’s most trusted lieutenants. During his two decades in the BSP, he thrice served as the leader of the opposition in the Uttar Pradesh legislative assembly. He joined the Bharatiya Janata Party months before it came to power, in 2017, and was labour minister in the first Adityanath government. Just before the 2022 assembly election, he broke with the BJP, accusing the party of neglecting Dalits, backward castes and farmers, and joined the Samajwadi Party. This, too, was short-lived, as he resigned in February 2024 to launch his own outfit, the Apni Janta Party.

With the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly election approaching, Swami Prasad has now set his sights on stitching together a “third front.” This year, he held a string of meetings with OBC and Dalit leaders who are not aligned with either the BJP or the Samajwadi Party—most notably the Nagina MP and Azad Samaj Party chief, Chandrashekhar Azad. Sunil Kashyap, a staff writer at The Caravan, spoke to Swami Prasad about his decades-long political evolution, the future of Bahujan politics and his reasons for proposing a third front in the upcoming election.

Could you tell us how your political journey began?

title: The spiritual cronyism of Narendra Modi and the BAPS
image_caption: Female staff working at the Eiffel Tower were removed, on the request of the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha, prompting a strike by site workers, causing a day-long closure of the global landmarkKenzo TRIBOUILLARD / AFP / Getty Images
content_html:
ON 5 SEPTEMBER, a visit by a delegation of clerics from the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha—a Hindu sect with deep ties to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh—to the Eiffel Tower in Paris led to a public controversy. According to local union representatives, female staff working at the monument were replaced by male colleagues or instructed to move away from their workstations as the delegation passed. The actions, at the request of the BAPS, prompted a strike by site workers, causing a day-long closure of the global landmark. French political leaders across the spectrum, including municipal officials, opposition leaders and national cabinet ministers, publicly condemned the arrangement as a violation of gender equality principles guaranteed under French law.

The next day, during the inauguration of a BAPS temple at Bussy-Saint-Georges, near Paris, Prime Minister Narendra Modi sent in a video message. “This grand Swaminarayan temple is a new milestone in the cultural relations between India and France,” he said. “Today, this stage has become an awakened platform for the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam”—a Sanskrit phrase, meaning that the world is one family, which the Modi government had made the slogan of its G20 presidency, in 2023. During an official visit to France, in June that year, Modi had met BAPS office-bearers, who showed him 3D renditions of the upcoming temple.

Despite this, and the well-known close linkages between Narendra Modi and the BAPS, the foreign-ministry spokesperson tried to delink the government from the controversy by claiming it to be a matter between two private entities. Modi’s participation by video, he suggested, was simply a customary expression of goodwill—a bureaucratically and politically neat evasion. The Indian embassy in Paris was closely involved with the inauguration ceremony of the temple and the whole French official ecosystem was aware of this deep association. The inauguration was already embedded in a major public-relations campaign that had gone on for nearly two weeks, and Modi’s participation conferred international legitimacy to it. Even after the misogynistic episode came to light, Vishal Sharma, the Indian ambassador to the Paris headquarters of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, publicly praised the BAPS. Later, he took more than fifty UNESCO diplomats from 43 countries for a special visit to the new temple.

The BAPS, under different circumstances, might have been considered a marginal religious organisation, but it has benefited enormously in the recent past due to the Modi government’s promotion of it as a benign and authentic expression of Indian civilisation in foreign countries. Its temples abroad are large and ornate, and its public-relations materials deploy the language of service, peace and cultural exchange. For most Indians who are not familiar with the BAPS, the organisation is perceived as a good vehicle for expanding India’s soft power abroad. The Eiffel Tower controversy, however, has thrown a spanner in the works. At the last moment, the BAPS had to cancel the grand parade meant to mark the end of the festivities, which began on 2 September and celebrated the birthday of its spiritual leader.

title: The strongman in contemporary fiction
content_html:
THERE WAS NO SHORTAGE of machismo at this year’s New Delhi World Book Fair. The theme was “Indian Military History: Valour & Wisdom @75.” There were men in fatigues, a pavilion with installations of tanks, jets and warships, and a tribute to Operation Sindoor. There were over a hundred events involving defence experts and former soldiers, and a visit from the chief of the army staff. Dharmendra Pradhan, the union minister for education at the time, inaugurated the fair and declared that “The Honourable Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modiji has transformed the culture of reading into a people’s movement.” The image of Modi was everywhere: from features already present in the book fairs of previous years, such as selfie points, to every promotional banner outside.

This scaffolding meant that the books, though everywhere, felt like a bit of a side act. That is not to say the fair did not see hordes of keen students, book lovers among the general public, or snotty intellectuals (I would really have liked to have been spared overhearing, in a queue, two Bengalis argue over whether Foucault or Derrida was more “grassroots,” for example.) But in the sense that a gathering focussed on books took on a different function, an officious one also visible in the Namo Book Festival in January—featuring over 400 books about Modi—where a book event is more a marketing fuss to promote the prime minister’s image. There is a lot of this around: a book exists to invite deification, sometimes quite literally.

A few years ago, Bluekraft’s Modi@20: Dreams Meet Delivery compiled articles praising Modi’s governance by ministers, a tech billionaire, a sportsman and an actor. One government of India blog, written by a young intern, said, “It’s no exaggeration to call it a guide like the Arthashastra for modern political aspirants.” The union home minister Amit Shah said, “This book will rise up to become equivalent to ‘Gita’ for those who believe in the path of building a complete persona and those who are in the field of social work and politics.” Meanwhile, the Bharatiya Janata Party’s Kerala unit accused Calicut University of being pro-Pakistan because it removed the book from its display of new books after two weeks, as it does with all newly released titles. The BJP state president said “the university authorities have insulted the Indian Constitution and the country’s democratic tradition.”

Six months after the book fair, at protests across the country, and online, Modi’s image was everywhere again, in placards, memes, graffiti, slogans and reels protesting against his government’s failures. This time, the theme was resentment and irreverence. A young man wandering around Jantar Mantar carried an X-ray report, trying to demonstrate that Modi’s chest is not 56 inches wide, as he had once claimed it to be. “Chhappan inch ka chhota bandar”—the 56-inch small monkey—was one of several older jibes to resurface, aimed at puncturing his carefully curated persona of a muscular leader.

title: How Trump is following Modi’s playbook on dealing with the media
image_caption: An activist group projects a message onto the CBS News headquarters to protest the Ellisons’ handling of the network.VALERIE TERRANOVA / GETTY IMAGES
content_html:
To many Indians, this story will sound familiar. An old, respected television news network ran afoul of its country’s right-wing government, which responded by criticising and investigating the channel. Officials declared that it was violating the law. They demanded it hand over millions of dollars. At first, the network’s owners were defiant—they declared that the government was infringing on press freedom and promised to continue reporting without fear or favour. But the channel’s leadership quietly started taking steps to mollify top officials. Executives pressured reporters to be less critical. Eventually, the owners sold off the network to oligarchs aligned with the state. Almost immediately, the network pushed out longtime staff, and its new editors reinvented it as a right-wing channel.

This is, of course, the story of NDTV. But it is also very similar to the story of CBS News in the United States. The channel angered Donald Trump with its coverage of his campaign and presidency, leading to an onslaught of threats and legal challenges. In 2025, the network was sold to a pair of Trump’s billionaire allies. It has since pivoted to a much more pro-Trump direction.

CBS is not an outlier. During Trump’s second term, his administration has assaulted US media outlets of all kinds. It has sued newspapers and television channels with reckless abandon and launched federal investigations into broadcasters. It has worked to strip away money from outlets and denied access to independent journalists. It has, in other words, almost perfectly followed the Narendra Modi government’s playbook. That does not mean US journalists are just as captured as their Indian counterparts. The United States still has a collection of large and small national outlets that aggressively report on Trump. However, in the less than two years since he returned to office, major publications and networks have started pulling punches or praising the president. Others have been hollowed out. The United States, then, is more than just following India’s path—it is speedrunning it.

No country has a perfect record on press freedom, but, for most of the last sixty years, the media atmosphere in the United States has been about as good as it gets. The first amendment to the US constitution guarantees freedom of speech and, thanks to several Supreme Court decisions, almost provides journalists with carte blanche to print and say whatever they wish. Journalists, for example, can report information that was obtained illegally as long as they did not commit crimes to get it. They can criticise the influential in extremely harsh terms—and even get facts incorrect—without facing sanctions, since defamation standards for public figures require plaintiffs to prove that the claim in question was not only harmful and false but that whoever uttered it knew that it was inaccurate. As a result, famous Americans rarely sue their critics.

title: Prashant Kishor’s Theory of Power Cannot Be Trusted
image_caption: Prashant Kishore addressing a “Bihar Badlao Rally”—Transform Bihar Rally—as president of the Jan Suraaj Party, on 11 April 2025 in Patna, Bihar.Santosh Kumar / HT Photo
content_html:
BY-ELECTIONS IN INDIA rarely make headlines. Yet, on the evening of 3 August, all news channels were tuned into the returns from the Bankipur by-election in Bihar, where Prashant Kishor, India’s best known political consultant, had been announced as the newly elected state legislator. Speaking to the press shortly after his victory, he sounded vindicated. “We have been saying this from day one: that the Bankipur election was not an election to elect an MLA. This was a verdict on BJP NDA government’s leadership in Bihar,” he said, referring to the Bharatiya Janata Party-led National Development Alliance government in Bihar, with the Janata Dal (United). Just months ago, the BJP had ousted the JD(U) supremo, Nitish Kumar—Bihar’s longest-serving chief minister and Kishor’s former client—and taken the chief ministership for itself. “The people of Bankipur, who have been Modi’s and BJP’s voters thus far, through this mandate they have sent a message to Modiji, that ‘We too have supported you,’” Kishor continued. “If you care so much for Gujarat, time has come that you also worry about the people of Bihar. You shouldn’t ask for votes in exchange for four kilos of grain or in the name of caste. Let’s talk about education and employment for Bihar. Let’s talk about how to stop the exodus of Bihar’s children.”

Seeing Kishor position himself against Narendra Modi’s leadership in this way and excoriate the NDA’s track record in Bihar, a lay observer could be forgiven for thinking that he had hitherto had no personal involvement with either. Yet, Kishor’s entry into public life had not only run parallel to but has been intimately tied up with Modi’s rise in national politics and the growing footprint of the BJP and its allies throughout the country. Bankipur is just over a hundred kilometres from Konar, a village in the Rohtas district where Kishor was born. Kishor’s journey back to his home state was long and meandering, taking many diversions and requiring him to wear different hats: public-health professional, high-level advisor in the Gujarat chief minister’s office, political consultant-at-large, JD(U) vice-president, the founder of a new political party and, now, a first-time state legislator.

I had been tracking Kishor and the political-consulting firm he founded, the Indian Political Action Committee, since 2015, when I was a doctoral student researching the professionalisation of Indian elections, focussing on the rising dominance of firms such as I-PAC. Even though he was by no means India’s first political consultant, by that point, Kishor’s name and organisation was virtually synonymous with the industry as a whole. He first caught public attention as the man behind the high-tech innovations of Modi’s 2014 prime-ministerial campaign. After Modi, Kishor worked for other big-time leaders, such as Nitish in Bihar, Mamata Banerjee in West Bengal, Amarinder Singh in Punjab and Jagan Mohan Reddy in Andhra Pradesh. 

“As someone who does not have a surname, it is very difficult to enter politics. No matter what the leaders say on the stage. You can enter as a karyakarta, but, to gain a foothold, to do something meaningful, there is very little option,” Kishor had observed, in 2019. “From Tamil Nadu to Kashmir, barring one or two exceptions, it is all closed at the top. It’s all meant for the families.” For a while, it seemed as though he was content with political-consulting firms. I-PAC was the vehicle through which he, and a new generation of young Indians, could enter the political arena without formally joining political parties or their frontal organisations. But after nearly a decade of working behind the scenes with politicians, in 2024, Kishor decided to throw his hat in the ring by launching the Jan Suraaj Party, one of India’s newest political outfits.
